title: From Topological Distance to Spatial Buffers: Efficient Halo Queries on Triangular DGGS
content: Discrete global grid systems (DGGSs) organize geographic data as indexed cells whose neighborhoods support spatial queries. We study exact halo construction on a triangular DGGS and its use in buffer coverage. Rather than store refined connectivity, the architecture reconstructs adjacency using compact integer triangular indices and an Atlas of Connectivity Maps. A graphics processing unit (GPU) resident hash frontier admits each new cell once. Probe reduction and reusable output staging reduce repeated work and delivery costs. Measurements through level 28 compare serial and twenty thread central processing unit (CPU) baselines using flat hash tables, on an Intel Core i7 12700K and NVIDIA RTX 4070. The largest halo contains 10.8 million cells and reaches page locked (pinned) host memory in 13.3 ms; its returned container copy is measured separately. Small queries favor CPU execution. Independent mesh references validate Pentakis adjacency, while the performance runs check cumulative output agreement. A stopping argument connects complete rings to conservative distance coverage, conditional on valid source and distance bounds. A separate World Geodetic System 1984 boundary buffer study includes source covering and distance filtering; CPU execution is faster in all seven cases. Numerical tests do not certify floating point distance bounds.
